Exploring the effects of gravity on a coflow
diffusion flame in an electric field
S. Karnani1, M. Schoen2, P. Coffin2, D. Dunn-Rankin1, F. Takahashi3,
Z-G. Yuan3 , D. Stocker2
1 Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
University of California, Irvine, CA 92697-3975
2 NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio 44135
3 National Center for Space Exploration Research on Fluids and Combustion, Cleveland, Ohio 44135
Fall Technical Meeting
of the Western States Section of the Combustion Institute
Hosted by the University of California, Irvine, CA
Oct 26-27, 2009

Electric Field Effects
Ion reactions make up a small subset of
combustion kinetics.
Microscopic electric field effects:
• Charge separation
•Acceleration prevented by collisions
with neutrals
• ~100 m/s ion drift velocity
Macroscopic field effects:
• Ion-driven wind (~1 m/s)
• Reshaping of the reaction zone
• Change in flame luminosity
Starik and Titova, 2002
• Altered stability
• Forced extinction

Flames and Body Forces
Instead of the classic teardrop shape, low-g flames 1g 0g
tend to exhibit a more spherical shape, owing to the
lack of buoyancy.
Effects of ion-driven convection are physically similar
to buoyancy.
• Natural convection complicates
the understanding of flame
0g w/ electric field
behavior!
Using both, the NASA 2.2-s
Drop Tower and the ISS
(proposed), we will study the
influence of chemi-ionization on
combustion without buoyancy.

Normal-Gravity Results (UCI)
• Looking at the transient data, high frequency
oscillations are present near saturation.
• The signal FFT hints to a beating phenomena with a
41Hz peak frequency.
• P-P oscillation is ~5% of the mean ion current.
• Flame images do not show signs of flame movement.
PMT signals can capture oscillations.
• Ion current variations lead PMT response.
Flame response time (100ms) >> Oscillation period (~25ms)

Normal-Gravity Results (UCI)
• Oscillation frequency abruptly
transitions from a 16.6Hz to
31.25Hz.
• Long exposure images show
the maximum and minimum of
flame oscillations.
• Transition accompanied by a
dramatic change in flame
shape.
Slideshow shows the following voltages:
100V increments: 0, -2000, -2800: -100: -4100

Normal and Low Gravity Results (NASA)
• Both normal and low-gravity testing
have similar behaviors
• Gravity appears to have a minimal
effect on the voltage-current
relationship for the flow conditions
studied

Coflow velocity will be reduced in future

Normal and Low Gravity Results (NASA)
•Flame has a 28Hz oscillation at -10kV
•Video framing rate is insufficient for
adequate tracking of the flame
oscillations.

Conclusions and Future Work
• Flame oscillations are present for a variety of applied field strengths.
• Field driven oscillations can be arranged into two regimes:
• Those which cause visible flame movement (~10 - 20Hz)
• Luminous oscillations (~30 - 40Hz region)
• Lower coflow velocities are necessary to recognize the contribution of buoyancy to
ionization.
